title: Wire EDM: program sim, setup sheet and tool list do not know a tool-less wire cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Part of #290. Found while working #532 (Wire EDM: 2-axis contour op).

**Background:** a Wire Contour (#532) mounts no library tool - the wire is the machine's EDM condition (#531) - so its `Operation::tool` is the empty word (`KindInfo::mounts_tool()` is false for the wire family). #532 taught the doors that create, generate, stamp, machine-check and post a wire cut. The surfaces below still read `op.tool` as a library tool. None of them crashes or posts anything (the program gate refuses a wire cut by name until #533), but what they say is wrong or unhelpful:

- **Program stock sim** (`crates/app/src/stock_sim.rs`, the plan walk): a wire cut stops the plan with `"<op>: tool  is not in the library"`. It should stay out of the dexel plan the way a probe and a torch do, by name ("a wire cut is verified by the wire laws, not the stock sim") - the wire's verdicts are #534's.
- **Setup sheet** (`crates/app/src/setup_sheet/operations.rs`, `tools.rs`): the op row prints an empty tool, and the tool table prints `(tool '' is no longer in the document)`. It should print the condition id, the wire diameter and the gap the machine states for it.
- **Tool list / tool-list export** (`crates/app/src/tool_list.rs`, `tool_list_export.rs`): a wire cut adds a row for the tool `""`. A wire EDM has no tool table; the row should not exist.
- **Other readers of `op.tool`** to audit for the same thing: `cutting.rs` (cutting data), `fixture_struck.rs`, `fixture_carried.rs`, `operation/footprint.rs`, `posting_index_swing.rs`, `tool_numbers.rs`.

**Not in this issue:** the wire verification laws themselves (#534) and the op / machine pages (#535).

**Done means:** on a document whose setup mounts a wire EDM and holds a generated Wire Contour: the program sim answers by name without "is not in the library"; the setup sheet shows the cut's condition, wire diameter and gap and no missing-tool line; the tool list has no row for it. Each pinned by a test in the owning crate's suite.

body:
Part of #290. Found while working #532 (Wire EDM: 2-axis contour op).

**What happens:** the Wire Contour operation (#532) is created and edited through the same undoable commands as every other kind (`CreateOperation`, `EditOperationParams`), and its parameters already ride the JSON door the MCP uses (`project::params_to_json` / `params_from_json`: `wire_contour { top_z, bottom_z, condition, side, start }`). But an agent cannot make one over MCP today:

- `add_operation` requires a non-empty `"tool"` (`mcp::tools::req_str`, and `"tool"` is in the schema's `required` list). A Wire Contour mounts no library tool - the wire is the machine's EDM condition (#531) - and `CreateOperation` refuses one that names a tool.
- No MCP tool mounts a machine file that states `edm.conditions`. The EDM templates are test fixtures, not library machines, until the wire post lands (#530's decision, #533), so a headless session has no wire EDM to create the op on.
- `list_operation_types` lists the kind with an empty `tool_kinds` and nothing that says "pass no tool"; the camcraft-mcp skill does not mention the kind.

**Expected:** `add_operation` with `kind: "Wire Contour"` and no `tool` (or an empty one), plus `params: { condition, side, start }`, creates the op on a setup that mounts a wire EDM; `edit_operation` patches `side`, `start` and `condition`; the refusals arrive as tool errors with the command's own words (no condition named, a condition with no gap or no wire diameter, a tool named on a wire cut).

**Scope:**
- `add_operation`: `tool` optional for a kind whose `KindInfo::mounts_tool()` is false; the schema's `required` and the description say so.
- A way to mount a wire EDM with a condition table in a headless session (the existing machine tool taking a `.mch` path, or the library entry once #533 adds it) - whichever exists when this is picked.
- `list_operation_types`: say that the kind mounts no tool.
- The camcraft-mcp skill: the kind, its fields, the "not exercised on a real EDM control" note (a process file: bump `PROCESS_VERSION`).

**Done means:** an MCP test (`crates/app/tests/mcp*.rs`) mounts a wire EDM with a synthetic condition table, adds a Wire Contour with no tool, edits its side, generates it, undoes and redoes; `add_operation` with a tool on that kind and with an unknown condition both return the command's refusal as a tool error.

title: Index swing check judges the tool against the swept work only: work swinging into the table, a fixture plate or a subplate is not judged

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Noted by the high-tier review of PR #1082 (review comment on that PR, head 642cd694); true on main before that PR as well, so not a regression of it.

**What.** The index-swing check (#804 / #810 / #818, `crates/app/src/posting_index_swing.rs`) judges the tool against the work as the rotary indexes. It does not judge the swept WORK (part, stock, and what turns with them) against what stands still under it: the machine table, a fixture plate, a rotary subplate. A long or wide workpiece on a low rotary can swing into the table or plate during an index and the program posts.

Related gap from the same review: a rotary standing directly on a fixture plate with no subplate is judged on the bare-table figure ("a plate alone raises nothing", by design) with no named note.

**Why P1, not P0, for now.** It is a collision the check does not look for, not one it looks for and gets wrong, and it is unknown how much of the table/plate geometry the check can read today (the machine file states `nose_to_axis`; the table's extent may not be stated at all). If the first step shows the figures are there and a real setup passes, re-rate it P0.

Done means: it is stated (decision file) what the swing check judges and against which bodies; the swept work's largest radius about the rotary line is judged against the stated distance from the centerline to the table / plate / subplate top, with a refusal by name when it does not clear and a named "not judged" note when the machine states no figure to judge it against; pinned by tests with a workpiece that clears and one that does not.

title: Add built-in vise: "Fit to the stock" fails with "invalid parameters: setup 'Setup1' has no stock" and the dialog never says the stock must be set first

body:
Reported by the maintainer in chat (2026-11-12, v0.18.0, with a screenshot), filed by an agent for him: "it is unclear how the built-in vise are supposed to work, and we cannot figure it out, we just get an error on fit to the stock".

**What he did.** New document, one setup (`Setup1`, active), a model imported (`Milling-test`), no stock defined yet (the browser still shows a `Stock` node under the setup). Fixtures -> Add built-in vise... -> picked "125 mm self-centering" -> left "Fit to the stock (centred, jaws closed on it)" ticked (the default) -> Place.

**What happens.** Nothing is placed. The dialog, the Fixtures page and the status bar all show, in red: `vise not placed: invalid parameters: setup 'Setup1' has no stock to fit the vise to`.

**Why.** `InsertVise::new` (`crates/app/src/commands/builtin_vise.rs`) with `VisePlacement::FitStock` reads `model::stock_world_aabb_for`, which is `None` while the setup's stock entity has no body. The refusal is right - there is nothing to fit to - but:
1. The dialog offers "Fit to the stock" ticked by default when the setup has no stock, and only says so after Place.
2. The message does not say what to do: set the stock first (Stock page), or untick the box and place the vise by position.
3. "invalid parameters:" is our word, not the user's; nothing he typed was invalid.
4. The dialog does not say how a built-in vise works at all: where it lands when fitted (fixed jaw against the stock's +Y side, centred in X, jaw floor under the stock, opening = the stock's Y width; a self-centering one centred in X and Y), what the figures mean for the fit, and that the placed vise is then judged in the collision checks.
5. The browser shows a `Stock` node for a setup whose stock has no body, so "has no stock" reads as wrong.

**Wanted**
- When the active setup has no stock body: the dialog says so before Place, in plain English ("This setup has no stock yet. Set the stock (Stock page) to fit the vise to it, or place the vise by position below."), with a button that opens the Stock page; "Fit to the stock" is off and greyed with that reason, and the position rows show.
- With a stock: one or two plain lines under the checkbox saying where the vise will land and how far the jaws open, from the stock's real figures (e.g. "Opens to 80.0 mm on the stock's Y width; stock sits on the jaw floor"), and a named refusal up front when the stock is wider than the vise's max opening.
- Refusal texts on this path lose the "invalid parameters:" prefix and say what to do next.
- The same for the two siblings that fail the same way: "Add mod vise pair" (`commands/mod_vise.rs`, "has no stock to fit the mod vise to") and parallels under the stock (`commands/accessory.rs`, "has no stock to fit the parallels under").
- A stock that has no body yet is shown as such in the browser (e.g. `Stock  not set`), the way `Machine  no machine` is.

Not wanted here: fitting the vise to the part instead of the stock, or creating a stock automatically - a vise holds the stock; if a default stock at import is wanted, that is its own issue.

Done means: on a setup without stock the dialog explains and offers the Stock page before any Place, and Place by position works; with a stock, Fit places the vise and the dialog said beforehand where; the three refusals read in plain English; pinned in the structural tests (labels, the greyed checkbox and its reason, the button) and by app tests for the refusal texts. No command semantics change; no snapshot PNG touched.

title: The browser (wasm32) build of CamCraft loads from the GitHub Pages site

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Asked for by the maintainer, 2026-11-12: "the wasm32 app should be loadable from the github pages for easy access". Filed by an agent for him (no `source:agent`: it is his request).

**Where things stand**
- GitHub Pages is now enabled for this repo (source: GitHub Actions) at https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/. The `site` and `pages` jobs of `release.yml` build the Zola site in `site/` and deploy it on a release tag (#688). The `github-pages` environment allows `v*.*.0` tags to deploy.
- The wasm32 shell runs in a browser on WebGL2 (#31, PR #847): `web/build-app-wasm.sh --release` writes `<target>/web/` with `index.html`, `wasi_shim.js`, `camcraft-ui.js` and `camcraft-ui_bg.wasm`. Nothing publishes that folder; today it only runs from a local http server.
- The site's front page already says the browser build comes "once the app and its interface build for the web".

**What is wanted**
The released wasm32 build is served from the Pages site, so anyone can open CamCraft in a browser from a link, without installing anything.
- The app lives under a fixed path of the site (e.g. `/Camcraft/app/`), with a clear link from the front page and the guide's first-run page.
- It is built in the release workflow from the tagged tree (a job that runs `web/build-app-wasm.sh --release` and hands its output to the `site` job, which places it in the Pages artifact) - **no new `push`, `pull_request` or `schedule` trigger** (Actions budget). Linux runner; say in the PR how many billed minutes it adds to a cut.
- Everything the page loads resolves under the project sub-path (`/Camcraft/app/...`, not `/`): the import map, `wasi_shim.js`, the `.js`/`.wasm` pair, any asset fetch. A fork's own Pages (another owner or repo name) must work too, as the `site` job's `--base-url` already does.
- The page says what it is: the version it was built from, that it runs in the browser on WebGL2, and what does not work there yet (the list on #31: file picker, playback without threads, WebGPU).
- A failed wasm build must not withhold the docs site or the release: the docs deploy without `/app/` and the run names what failed (the way `publish` treats a failed platform build).

**Known obstacles**
- #949: the build script rewrites the checkout's `Cargo.lock`; in CI that must not leak into anything packaged from the same checkout.
- `.wasm` size and Pages limits (1 GB site, 100 MB per file): state the size in the PR; use `wasm-opt` if it is needed and available without a new unpinned download.
- Pages serves no custom headers (no COOP/COEP), so nothing may depend on `SharedArrayBuffer` / threads.

Done means: after a release tag, `https://neotech.github.io/Camcraft/app/` loads the shell of that release in a current Chrome and Firefox, linked from the site's front page; pinned by a check in the workflow that the Pages artifact holds `app/index.html` and the `.wasm`, and by a test or script check that the page's URLs are relative to its own folder.

Part of #688 (docs and browser build on Pages); builds on #31 (the app and UI on wasm).

title: Lathe holder body: the reach law reads the body at |X + x|, which is only right for a tool on the positive-X side

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Noted by the high-tier review of PR #1043 (review comment on that PR, head 1a6d4017). The law is on main (#369); PR #1043 is what first lets a user reach it.

**What.** `Reach::radii` reads a lathe holder body point at radius `|X + x|`, where `X` is the tool tip's signed radial position and `x` the body point's radial offset in the turning tool frame. The UI and MCP wording says "+x points away from the spindle axis". Both are true only for a tip at X >= 0.

- Facing a little past centre (tip at a small negative X): `X + x` is still the body's real position, so the reading is right; only the wording is loose.
- A tool that really sits on the other side of the axis (a rear turret or gang position programmed at negative X), if any turning path can carry one: the body would be read mirrored through the axis, so a holder that hits could be judged clear.

**Not known.** Whether any turning operation or machine definition today can put a tip at a negative X other than the facing overrun. If none can, this is a wording fix plus a guard; if one can, it is a collision-law defect and should be re-rated P0.

Done means: it is stated (with a test) which signed-X cases the turning generators can produce; the law either handles a tip on the negative side correctly or refuses it by name; the UI/MCP wording says what +x means for both cases.

title: A stock-from-model's source model left in the tree is judged as a part: the program verdict reports a gouge for any cut into the casting

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while reproducing #1091 (and the reason the #1077 reviewer's probe got a second, unrelated refusal).

**What happens.** Import a casting, set the stock to "from model" with that casting as its source, import the part, and machine it. The casting stays in the tree as a model, and `stock_sim::part_facets_as_modelled` reads every non-fixture model as the part. So the program verdict judges the casting as finished geometry, and any cut into it - every cut, since the casting is the stock - is a gouge: `post blocked - gouge: program cuts below the model in 812 cell(s), worst 20.00 mm at (-1.75, -7.75, z 10.00)` (a Bore of a 16 mm hole in a part under a stepped casting, fixture of `crates/app/tests/stepped_stock_rapid.rs` without its `DeleteEntity` of the casting).

**Expected.** A model that is only the source of a `FromModel` stock is stock, not part: the verdict (and the field view) should not read it as finished geometry. (Possibly: a model that is the source of the stock and is not the source of any operation.)

**Workaround in the #1091 tests.** Delete the casting after `SetStock` - the stock keeps its own copy of the facets.

Done means: a casting used as from-model stock and left in the tree posts a legal program over a separate part, pinned by a test; a model that is both the stock source and an op's source (`edge_break_gate.rs`'s brick) keeps today's verdict.

body:
**What:** `solid_law_goldens::every_posted_golden_is_a_program_the_gate_passes` (#862, #1000) judges every posted `.nc` golden whose stem has a `.cl` golden. Since #1000 its `UNJUDGED` list holds one entry: `arc_planes`. That program is hand-built in `crates/app/tests/arc_planes.rs` (a G18 and a G19 arc between XY arcs, for the five dialect posts). No operation kind, part, region or tool record makes it, so no gate a user's post runs can judge it. The guard can't tell a synthetic posting fixture from an op program nobody judged, so it keeps a by-name exception list.

**Why it matters:** a by-name exception list is where an unjudged op golden can hide later. A synthetic fixture should say what it is in the golden itself, the way a refused program carries the "refused program, posted for syntax conformance" first line.

**Done means:** posted goldens of hand-built posting fixtures (today `arc_planes` in Fanuc, haas, mazak, sinumerik, heidenhain) carry a first-line marker the guard recognises (e.g. "synthetic program, posted for syntax conformance"), written by the suite's regeneration path (`WRITE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test -p camcraft-app --test arc_planes`) and not by hand. Alternatively the fixture gets a part and a gate that judges it. `UNJUDGED` is then empty and removed, so any new unjudged posted golden fails the guard.

Found by the #1000 worker. Part of #1000's follow-up.

title: Rapid-in-stock law reads the stock's highest point everywhere: a legal entry dive over a lower part of a stepped stock is refused

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found by the high-tier review of PR #1077 (review comment on that PR, head c6c658db). Present on main for part-sourced Bores; PR #1077 extends the same reading to stock-sourced Bore and Thread.

**What happens.** Verify's rapid law (#96, `RapidInStock`) caps the stock column at the flat `stock_top_z`, the highest point of the whole stock. On a stock that is not a flat-topped box - a "from model" casting or a carried stock with a boss - a rapid down to just above a lower surface is judged as if the stock stood at its highest point there too.

Reviewer's probe: stock solid to Z 20 over the hole's mouth, with a boss to Z 30 elsewhere. A Bore on that hole (part-sourced and stock-sourced alike) rapids from clearance to Z 22, 2 mm above the real stock under it, and is convicted `RapidInStock { at: 0 }`. The post is blocked for a legal program.

**Expected.** The law reads the stock's top at the rapid's XY (the local column), not the global maximum. A rapid that ends above the stock really under it passes; a rapid into stock that really stands there is still convicted.

**Why P1.** It refuses, it does not gouge - but a user with a casting or a stepped stock cannot post a correct program. The probe also imported the casting as a model, which added a gouge refusal of its own, so the first step is a clean reproduction with stock only.

**Careful.** This is a gouge law: loosening it must not let any rapid into real stock pass. Carried stock, a faced top (`acquit_by_prior`), the 3+2 site and Thread's descent all read the same cap.

Done means: a pinning test with a stepped stock where the dive over the low part passes and the same dive over the boss is convicted, for a part-sourced and a stock-sourced Bore; the existing rapid-law tests (`ladder_entry_height`, the #96 pins) unchanged.

title: UI: native Open/Save dialogs can open behind the app window

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
## What

Every native picker (Open, Model, Save, Save As, Post, machine/post/theme picks) could
open **behind** the CamCraft window: the rfd dialog was created without an owner, and the
shell never asked for the foreground. A dialog opened right after launch — when the app was
started from a terminal or a script — was the worst case: the shell itself was not the
foreground window, so neither it nor its dialog was visible.

Reproduced on Windows 11 at 125 % scaling with the v0.18.0 release build: launch the app,
press Ctrl+O, and the `#32770` "Open" dialog exists but sits under the shell.

## Why

`crates/ui/src/file_dialog.rs` built `rfd::FileDialog` with title/filters/directory only —
`set_parent` was never called, so Windows had no owner to keep the dialog above. The shell
also never called `focus_window`, so a launch from a terminal left the app behind it, and an
owned dialog follows its owner's place in the z-order.

## Done means

- The shell asks for the foreground once, after the window is created.
- Every native picker is owned by the shell window, and the owner is raised just before the
  dialog opens.
- The GPU refusal `MessageDialog` is owned too.
- Hand-checked: launch from a terminal, first Ctrl+O, the dialog is visible in front; repeat
  for Save and Model.

Native dialog ownership has no headless test: rfd modals are hand-test-only in this repo
(`egui_app/tests.rs` says so), so the evidence is the hand check plus the z-order probe.

title: A matched drill is falsely convicted of a gouge on a reduced-fidelity model flagged above ~0.0105 mm

labels.name: in-review

labels.name: source:agent

body:
Found while working #904 (pinning the containment solid law on a reduced-fidelity model). This is in the code PR #911 merged; #904's slice does not change it.

**What happens.** A drill matched to its hole, on a model flagged between about 0.0105 mm and 0.015 mm (the refusal bound), is convicted with `Gouge` at its first plunge, even when it stops well above the hole's floor. The gate then blocks the post with a gouge that is not there. Below about 0.0105 mm (a metre-unit file's 0.01 mm included) and at full fidelity it is clean.

**Repro.** A 40 x 40 x 20 block with a 20 x 20 blind hole to Z 10, a 4 mm drill (`DR-0400`), one `Hole { radius: 2.0, entry_z: 20.0, floor_z: 10.0 }`, Bottom Z 10.2:

| model imported at | blocking warnings |
|---|---|
| full fidelity, 0.008 ... 0.0105 mm | none |
| 0.011 mm, 0.012 mm, 0.0149 mm | `Gouge { at: 1 }` |
| 0.03 mm (refused by name at the gate) | none |

(`crates/app/tests/coarse_contain.rs` on #904's branch has the fixture; pass `Some(0.011)` and a bottom of 10.2.)

**Likely cause.** The section law (b) reads `floor = r - leave - cx.tightened(cx.gouge_tol)` (`sim` `verify/section.rs`). `GOUGE_TOL` exists to absorb the chord error of our own regions (`operation/material.rs`: "half the geo2d round-join chord error plus room for float chains"). A drill's region is the hole's rim as a polygon, so a matched drill's centre stands a few microns inside `r` by construction. Once the model's excess has taken more than about half the tolerance, what is left no longer covers that polygon's own sagitta, and the law convicts the drill against its own rim. The same may hold for other kinds whose regions carry our own chords (bore, thread mill, circular).

**What is owed.** Decide how law (b) should split its tolerance between our own discretization and the model's excess (for example: tighten only the part of the tolerance not spent on the region's own chord error, or build these rims finer), so an honest drill is not convicted on a model that is still judged.

**Done means:** a matched drill, bore and thread mill on a model flagged anywhere below the refusal bound verify clean, with a pin at 0.0149 mm; a real gouge there is still convicted.

body:
Part of #361. Related: #864 (reduced-fidelity models), #904 (laws on a reduced-fidelity part).

**What happens.** A STEP that can only be meshed coarser than the importer promises (over the facet budget) is refused as a tool body by name (`tool_body_file::accept`): the collision laws read a body's envelope with no allowance for its chord error, and a coarse holder reads smaller than the holder is. That is safe, but vendor assemblies are often detailed (threads, lettering, small fillets), and the user's only way forward is to simplify the model elsewhere.

**Fix.** Take the body with its achieved chord error and judge it larger by that much: grow the spindle body's envelope bands (`HolderProfile`) radially and at both ends, and the lathe body's clearance spans (`LatheClearance`) on every side, by the excess over the importer's promise. Carry the chord on the body (project file too) and show it in the editor ("judged 0.04 mm larger"). Keep the refusal past a stated cap.

**Done means:** a body imported over budget lands, its judged envelope is never smaller than the full-fidelity one's (pinned by comparing the two on a curved fixture forced over budget), and a collision the full-fidelity body convicts is still convicted.

Part of #361. Found while making lathe holder bodies reachable from the tool editor and MCP.

**What happens.** A turning tool can carry a lathe holder body (#369), and every move is judged against the part and the standing stock (`operation/turning_holder.rs`: "What stands. title: M12.1: machining mesh - crafted records that provoke every solidcore-tess shortfall, and a proven deviation bound for spline faces

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Follow-up of #940 (machining mesh seam, PR stacked on #941).

What #940 delivers: `camcraft_kernel::machining_mesh` refuses by name every `PlanStats` shortfall that touches the guarantee (unmeshed, lenient, unsampled edge, a face or edge capped off its tolerance), pinned by `every_planner_shortfall_is_a_refusal_or_a_note` on SYNTHETIC `PlanStats` values; and a SAMPLED deviation (15 barycentric points a triangle), judged by the closed-form distance to the record's analytic surface where the face is analytic, else by the parametric distance |S(u,v) - T(u,v)|.

Owed:
1. **Real provocations.** No fixture under testdata/models makes the planner report any shortfall (checked at 0.005, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0002 and 0.0001 mm on Milling-test.step and sample_ap214.step). Build small crafted records (a pcurve off its edge, a free edge, a face whose grid must be thinned past `MAX_FACE_GRID`, an edge past 20 000 nodes) and pin that each reaches its named `MeshRefusal` through `machining_mesh`, not only through `judge_stats`.
2. **Spline and revolved faces.** They are judged only by the parametric distance, which over-reads on a non-uniform parameterisation (a few per cent on a rational circle) - a possible false refusal. Add a projection onto the plan surface (Newton from the sample's (u, v)) so they get a true distance, with a fixture that has such a face.
3. **Between the samples.** The deviation is a sampled maximum, a lower bound of the true one; solidcore-tess meshes right up to the tolerance (0.993 of it on Milling-test). Either a stated bound on the sag between samples, or a margin in the seam, so "within" is a guarantee.

What upstream solidcore-tess would need (for the maintainer to raise; not filed upstream): a cancellation hook in `plan`; a per-face measured sag in `PlanStats` for every face; a stated bound on the sag between the planner's sample points.

Everything stays inside `crates/kernel`. Part of #27. Gates #917.

Done means: each shortfall entry is pinned by a crafted record through `machining_mesh`; a non-analytic face is judged by a projected distance with a fixture; the decision file says what bounds the sag between samples.

title: Adaptive plans differ across platforms on the same commit (likely libm last-place rounding)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Found while working #984.

**What happens:** the same commit plans the same part differently on two platforms. `app pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (release) on ecb54b7f:

| platform | rings levels | moves / planar / arcs |
|---|---|---|
| Windows (the #850 measure, PR #865) | Z 20.000 | 5530 / 5497 / 600 |
| macOS, Apple silicon (Homebrew rustc 1.99.1) | Z 20.000 (crossing at -2.33, -2.78) | 5786 / 5753 / 651 |

macOS is deterministic run to run, so it is not hash-map order. Rust does not contract `a*b+c` into FMA unless asked, so the most likely cause is the platform libm: `f64::sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `hypot`, `exp`, `powf` call the system math library (MSVC CRT, glibc, Apple libm), which are not correctly rounded and differ in the last place. The STEP tessellation and the adaptive planner both use them, and the planner's crossing and acceptance tests are knife edges a 16 nm change flips (#882, #982). Not yet confirmed which call sites diverge, and not run on Linux.

**Why it matters:** a toolpath (and so the posted G-code) for the same part, tool and parameters depends on the OS the user runs. Every output is still verified and a crossing plan is refused by name, so this is not a gouge; but golden counts and exact plan pins cannot hold across platforms, and a user can see a different path from the same project file on two machines.

**Possible directions (open):** route the geometry and planner transcendental calls through a pure-Rust deterministic libm (the `libm` crate is already in Cargo.lock) so every platform rounds the same; or make the planner's decisions robust to sub-micron perturbation (#882, #982). Either changes toolpaths and needs every adaptive fixture re-measured.

Done means: the cause is confirmed on a second platform (Windows or Linux run of the bore test, plus which calls diverge), and either the output is made platform-identical with goldens re-measured, or the decision not to is recorded.

Refs #984, #882, #982.

body:
Part of #894.

A thread mill is not centre-cutting, and the thread-milling ride (`machining2d::thread_ride`) feeds it down the hole's axis before the first lead-in arc. That is air only if an earlier operation opened the hole. Nothing checks it: the `Thread` operation generates and verifies clean on a part whose hole is modelled, even when the program holds no drilling operation before it and the stock at the hole is solid. The gouge laws read the part (the hole is in the model), so they see nothing; the centre-cutting audit (`operation::plunge_solid`, `camcraft_motion::plunge_law`) is not asked for this kind, and it reads the raw stock, which would refuse every thread.

**Effect:** forget the tap drill and the program plunges a thread mill into solid metal at plunge feed - a broken cutter, with no finding at generate, at verify or at the post gate.

**Fix sketch:** read the stock the setup's earlier operations leave standing (the prior grid the drilling laws already read, `operation::drill_prior`) under each threaded hole: the tool's full cylinder down the axis and the first pass's lead-in must fall through air. Refuse by name at generate ("the hole at (x, y) is not drilled yet - add a drilling operation before the thread") and digest the program ahead in the stamp, so reordering the operations marks the thread Stale.

**Done means:** a Thread operation with no drilled hole under it is refused by name; the same operation after a Drill of at least the tool's diameter generates; moving the Drill after the Thread turns it Stale and refuses; pinned by an app test. The milled `Bore` ride's axis entry gets the same reading or its own issue.

Found while working #882 (held branch `issue/882-adaptive-open-simplify` @ 70ac996f; see https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/issues/882#issuecomment-6811353217).

**What happens:** `adaptive/lift.rs` `lift_returns` keeps the microlifted plan only when its worst reading is not above the spiral's, and both are read in half-degree steps. On main, the 60 x 14 slot reads 48.0 against 48.0. Any geometry perturbation, even a 16 nm thinning of the opening, makes the spiral read 47.5, so the lifted plan is dropped and the slot falls from HSM (15.7 % load) to Offset rings.

Done means: the acceptance compares within a stated tolerance, not on equal half-degree steps. A pinning test shows the slot keeps the same plan under a perturbation of the opening's area in the 16 nm to 0.25 um range, and no adaptive fixture's verdict changes on main.

Found by the STEP bench of #916 (`crates/kernel/tests/step_agreement.rs`), at the solidcore pin `55d0e7638b9e1ebbf91ab8c10657e595c114ecda`.

**1. Wrong bounding box (the one that matters).**
`testdata/models/Milling-test.step` (and its inch twin) is a 60 mm disc with a flat at Y = 19.719. Imported through `camcraft_kernel::solidcore_step`, the solid's volume (52808.744 mm^3) and area (11143.378 mm^2) agree with truck's mesh to 1.2e-4, but `StepSolid::measure`'s box - the port's `calculate_bounding_box` with `tight: true` - is `[-30, -30, -5]..[30, 30, 20]`. The file's own vertices, truck's mesh and solidcore's own mesh (`solidcore-tess`) all stop at Y = 19.719. The box takes the whole R = 30 cylinder, not the trimmed face. It is pinned in the bench as `disagree: bounding box`.

Not known yet: whether the port's box is wrong for any trimmed periodic face, or whether the record-to-kernel build (`solidcore_convert::brep::to_kernel_body`) gives the face a parameter box that covers the whole circle. A kernel-made fixture (a cylinder cut by a plane through the seam's own booleans) would tell the two apart.

Why P1: stage 5 (#917) puts imported geometry under every toolpath. A box 10 mm too large would mis-size automatic stock and mis-place anything aligned to the part's extent.

**2. Stale cached topology after the build.** `to_kernel_body` hands out a B-rep whose cached `Face::shell` is behind its face-use links on every fixture; the port's `topology::integrity::check` refuses it ("cached face shell: face 0 not found"). The seam works around it with `Brep::refresh_cached_topology()` (public; rewrites the cached fields only). To report upstream (tangency-labs/solidcore); the maintainer decides who files it there.

**3. No cancellation in the STEP topology pass.** `solidcore_step::topology::read_solids` takes no progress or cancel hook, so the importer's time bound cannot stop it; it is bounded only by the reader's caps and the seam's 64 MiB size bound. To raise upstream, or to bound by calling the per-solid readers from the seam.

Part of #27. Gates #917.

title: Work offsets: core uses an index, the post supplies the word and display name

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server and agent tooling (crates/app/src/mcp, camcraft-mcp skill)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
## Problem

A setup stores its work offset as an index (`SetupDef::work_offset`), but core
turns that index into a Fanuc-style word before any post is involved:

- The table `WCS_SLOTS = ["G54".."G59"]` lives in `camcraft-app`
  (`operation/types/sel.rs`) and is read directly by the Setups page combo,
  `setup::wcs_label`, the setup sheet, the MCP `set_work_offset` tool and the
  refusal messages.
- `posting::wcs_context` writes the word, not the index, into the stream as
  `PARAM WorkOffset`. Posts then parse it back: Fanuc and Mazak use
  `slotOf("G55") -> 1`, Heidenhain regex-matches `^G5([4-9])$` to pick a preset
  row.
- An index of 6 or more is refused in core, so extended offsets
  (`G54.1 P..`, Sinumerik `G505+`, further Heidenhain preset rows) cannot be
  expressed.

A setup with no machine and no post still shows `G54`: the word comes from
neither. Every other ask in the stream is already dialect-neutral (coolant,
after-operation); the work offset is the exception.

## Proposal

1. **Stream carries the index.** `PARAM WorkOffset` becomes a 1-based number.
   A manifest flag (`workOffsetIndex = true`) opts a script in, following the
   `coolantModes` / `afterModes` pattern. A script without the flag keeps
   receiving the word for offsets 1-6, so user-loaded posts keep working, and
   is refused by setup name for any offset above 6.
2. **Each post maps the index to its own word** and refuses, by setup name,
   an index it cannot express. The limit becomes the post's, not core's.
3. **The post supplies the display name.** A script may define a function
   (for example `workOffsetName(n)`) returning what the control calls offset
   `n` ("G55", "G54.1 P3", "preset 2"). The UI, setup sheet, MCP tool and
   refusal messages show "WCS n (name)" for the setup's resolved post.
4. **Fallback.** A script that defines no name function shows plain "WCS n".
5. **Core and UI speak indexes.** `WCS_SLOTS` leaves `camcraft-app` and
   `camcraft-ui`, apart from the two pre-v54 file migrations that need the old
   words to read old files.

## Out of scope

- The project file format: it already stores the index, so no version step.
- The legacy `G54` entity name of a document without setups (internal name
  only; renaming it would need a migration for no user benefit).
- Rotated work offsets (#315, #760).

## Open questions

- Where the name lookup lives so the layering holds (ui -> app -> post): an
  app-level function that evaluates the setup's post, with caching, since the
  UI must not evaluate scripts per frame.
- The MCP tool's input: accept an index, and keep accepting the old words as
  aliases for 1-6?
- Whether the six-offset cap is replaced by a per-post maximum the script
  declares, so the combo can list the right number of entries.
- Whether the simulator or any test harness parses the posted offset word
  back; not yet checked.

## Acceptance

- Every existing posted-program golden is byte-identical (the 148 that
  contain a `G5x` word included).
- Every shipped `.cps` declares the flag and maps the index itself; no
  `slotOf`-style parsing of a word remains.
- A setup can be given offset 7 or higher and posts correctly on a dialect
  that supports it; a dialect that does not refuses by setup name.
- A user post without the flag posts offsets 1-6 exactly as before.
- The Setups page shows the resolved post's name for each offset, and
  "WCS n" when the post supplies none.
- `docs/CNC-INTERMEDIATE.md` and `assets/posts/AGENTS.md` describe the new
  value, flag and name function.

## Related

Background (closed):

- #196 and #342 introduced the current design: G54-G59 is the setup's post
  label.
- #51 added Heidenhain preset selection for other work offsets - the source
  of the `G5x` -> preset-row regex.
- #876 already called "work offset word" jargon in the UI.

Open work this touches:

- #836 (TinyG post) and #728 (Sienci AltMill on the grblHAL post) add new
  `.cps` files that would need the flag and the mapping.
- #258 (Post dialog) touches the same post-options area.
- #760 (rotated work offset) touches the WCS code; rotation stays out of
  scope here.

body:
Found while working #864 (a STEP model imported coarser than the importer promises is flagged, its gouge verdicts tightened, and refused past that).

**What #864's PR does.** A reduced-fidelity model carries its achieved error. The gouge laws of the upright mill kinds subtract the excess from their tolerance while a positive tolerance is left: the section law (b), the solid law (b2), the envelope law's gouge half (f), `generate::contain_into`, the lathe's axial hole verdict, and the program sim's deviation tolerance. Past that, the program gate refuses by name.

**What is owed.** Everything below is safe today (refused, or stricter than before), but less useful than it should be.

1. **Kinds refused outright on any reduced-fidelity model**, because their gouge laws do not read the excess yet (`operation::fidelity_law::excess_aware`):
   - the cone and engrave rides: 2D chamfer, deburr, trace, engrave (generator construction laws);
   - probe, and the cross drill (`operation/cross_part.rs`, `SolidLaw { allow: GOUGE_TOL }`);
   - the multi-axis kinds (`motion` `multiaxis/entry_ramp.rs`, `stamp*.rs`, `rotary_links.rs`) and the rotary kinds (`operation/rotary_law.rs`, `allow` and `rapid_allow`);
   - turning (`motion` `turning/revolve.rs`, `form.rs`, `thread.rs`; `blade_warnings`, `thread_warnings`, `form_warnings`);
   - plasma.
   Each needs `material.excess` threaded into its law and the kind added to `excess_aware`. A metre-unit STEP file is always reduced fidelity (next point), so these kinds cannot post on one today.
2. **Collision laws are not tightened**: shank and holder reach (`sim` `verify/reach.rs`), rapids in stock (`verify/rapids.rs`, `rapids_posed.rs`, `rapids_radial.rs`), the turning rapid, bar-feed and holder scans (`margin: GOUGE_TOL` in `generate.rs`). They judge clearance against rest material. While an operation still posts the excess is under 0.01 mm, so a clearance can read up to that much too generous on a convex wall.
3. **A metre-unit STEP file** stops at the kernel's least tolerance (1e-5 m = 0.01 mm, #839) and is flagged reduced fidelity with half the verdict tolerance left. Scaling the geometry to millimetres before meshing would remove the cause.

6. **The envelope law (f) and the containment solid law** are tightened through the same helper as (b) but have no fixture-level pin of their own on a reduced-fidelity model.

Done means: each kind in (1) is either judged with tightened laws or stays refused for a stated reason; the laws in (2) grow their bands by the excess; (3) and (4) are decided and built or closed with the reason; pins for (6).

title: Program units are a document setting: every post writes mm or inch from the document, not from the machine file

body:
Maintainer decision (2026-11-11, in chat, on #901): "the units should come from a 'global setup' rather than a localized setup with operations or the machine settings.. all machines can handle mm and inch and degrees and radians.. just a matter of post output.. that setting should come from a global setting for the document rather than machine or post."

Today: the posted unit comes from the machine file (`kinematics.default.units.length` -> `machine.units`), and only the three Tormach posts read it. The document's Units choice (`SetUnits`, a radio on the Stock page) is display-only. So the user cannot find where the program's unit is set, and most posts cannot post inch at all.

Wanted:
- One document-level setting decides the unit of the posted program for every post. Recommended: the document's existing Units choice (`SetUnits`, already saved in the project file and already an undoable command with history) becomes the program unit too - one setting, not two. A second, separate derivation anywhere (machine file, post option, setup, operation) is a bug.
- The machine file's `units.length` only says which unit the file's own numbers are written in (the parser already scales them to mm); it no longer chooses the program unit. The Tormach posts switch from `machine.units` to the document's unit.
- Every post writes the program in the document's unit: inch = lengths / 25.4 at four decimals, feeds and other length-bearing words converted, and the dialect's unit word (G20 / G21, Heidenhain G70 / G71, Sinumerik G70 / G71 or G700 / G710) in the opening block. A post whose control cannot run a unit (Carvera's firmware halts on G20) refuses that document by name instead.
- The setting lives where a user looks for a document-wide choice (not only on the Stock page), and the post dialog states the unit the program will be written in.
- MCP: the existing units tool (or a new one, `area:mcp`) covers it; `EndUnits` (#596) keeps working against the document's unit.

Open point for the maintainer: angles. Every post writes rotary words in degrees today and nothing in the document chooses an angle unit. If a document-level angle unit (degrees / radians) is wanted for display or output, say so and it is filed as its own issue; it is not part of this one.

Depends on #901 (each post states the unit it writes) - land that first.

Done means: with the document set to inch, each shipped post either writes a correct inch program with its unit word (golden per post, numbers checked against the mm golden / 25.4) or refuses by name; with it set to mm, output is unchanged apart from #901's unit word; no post reads `machine.units` for the program unit; the setting is reachable at document level in the UI and through MCP.

title: STEP import refuses a valid HOOPS Exchange file: ruststep cannot parse an empty parameter list `()` — one entity kills the whole DATA section, and the error points at the wrong line

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
## What happens

Opening `4B52391_step_conversion_r_0.step` (16.5 KB, exported by HOOPS Exchange 2026.7) in CamCraft v0.17.0 fails with:

```text
corrupt STEP: syntax error: Error while tokenizing STEP input

0: at line 20, in Tag:
DATA;
^
```

Other STEP readers open the file without complaint (SolidCraft among them). The part is a plain `ADVANCED_BREP / MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP / CLOSED_SHELL` with 13 faces — nothing exotic.

The error is also misleading: line 20 is just the `DATA;` keyword line. Delete the HOOPS comment from the header and the error "moves" to line 18 — it always lands on `DATA;`, which never misled *me* to the header. The real defect is deep inside the DATA section, at entity `#11` (line 435):

```step
#11=DRAUGHTING_MODEL('',(),#10);
```

## Reproduction

1. Get a STEP file exported by HOOPS Exchange (a very common commercial SDK; lots of cloud converters route through it) — or use the 9-line file below.
2. `File → Open` in CamCraft, or call `camcraft_app::geometry::import::load_model` headless.
3. Expected: the part loads. Actual: `corrupt STEP: syntax error … at line 20, in Tag: DATA;`.

Minimal repro (a whole valid STEP file — this reproduces the exact symptom):

```step
ISO-10303-21;
HEADER;
FILE_DESCRIPTION(('test'),'2;1');
FILE_NAME('repro','2026-11-11T00:00:00','','');
FILE_SCHEMA(('AUTOMOTIVE_DESIGN'));
ENDSEC;
DATA;
#1=A('',(),#2);
ENDSEC;
END-ISO-10303-21;
```

Remove the `()` from `#1` and it loads. That one construct is the whole bug.

## Root cause — an upstream ruststep bug, not a bad file

ISO 10303-21 defines `list = "(" [ parameter { "," parameter } ] ")"` — the empty list `()` is legal. ruststep 0.4.0 (the latest release, Sep 2024) parses lists with `list()` → `comma_separated(parameter)`, and its `separated` combinator is `tuple((f, many0(sep+f)))` — **at least one element required**. So `()` never parses, anywhere.

- Upstream status: [ricosjp/ruststep#256](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/issues/256) (open, filed Feb 2026) reports the same bug against the released crate. The fix is *already on upstream main* — [`90fdc935` "fix(exchange): handle empty parameter lists"](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/commit/90fdc9351746f1f1d1e435b88f15371edaaaa14d) (Feb 2025) wraps the element list in `opt_(...)` and adds an `empty_parameter_list` test — but it has never shipped: the newest crates.io release is still 0.4.0 (Sep 2024), which predates it. So the one-line fix exists; it just needs a pin.
- Why the error message is wrong: `entity_instance_list` is `many0_(entity_instance)`, so parsing silently *stops* at `#11`; then the `ENDSEC;` tag fails, `data_section` fails, and the outer `many0_(data_section)` in `exchange_file` **discards that failure and yields zero sections** — the last error nom keeps is the `END-ISO-10303-21;` tag check, which lands on `DATA;`. Hence "line 20".

Bisection evidence (v0.17.0 code paths, headless):

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| original file | `corrupt STEP … at line 20, in Tag: DATA;` |
| header comment removed | same failure, now "line 18" — header is innocent |
| `#11`'s `()` replaced by `(#10)` | **loads fine — 164 facets** |
| 9-line minimal repro with `()` | fails with the identical wrong-line symptom |

Roughly 400 of the file's 416 DATA entities use no empty lists; the single `DRAUGHTING_MODEL('',(),#10)` — an entity that isn't even geometry — is enough to reject the entire part.

## Proposed fixes (not exclusive)

1. **Short term, smallest real fix:** `[patch.crates-io]` ruststep to an upstream git rev that includes [`90fdc935`](https://github.com/ricosjp/ruststep/commit/90fdc9351746f1f1d1e435b88f15371edaaaa14d) (upstream main still declares `version = "0.4.0"`, so CamCraft's direct dep *and* truck-stepio's `ruststep = "0.4"` both resolve to the patched crate unchanged; pin a `rev`/`tag` for reproducibility). If a git dependency is not wanted, the fallback is a small fork + `[patch.crates-io]`, or preprocessing `()` — but that's text-hacking around a parser bug. Bonus either way: pin the 9-line repro (or the real file) as a regression test asset so whichever route taken can't silently regress when ruststep finally releases.
2. **Error UX regardless:** when STEP import fails, say *where parsing stopped* (entity `#11` here) rather than a line number in the header, and say the file may well be valid — currently "corrupt STEP" sends users to re-export blindly. Since ruststep's `VerboseError` swallows the inner failure, even a cheap second pass ("re-parse entity by entity to find the first failing one") would beat today's message.
3. **Long term:** #27 (Solidcore replaces the B-rep engine) makes the whole ruststep/truck-stack class of import failures go away — this is one more data point for why that milestone matters.

(I've kept the original failing file offline since it contains my part geometry — happy to share it with a maintainer privately if that helps; the 9-line repro above reproduces the identical failure.)

title: Adaptive growth planner: the ring opening is quadratic in outline vertices - one level of the user's STEP bore grows for ~200 s

labels.name: blocked
labels.description: Waiting on another issue or a decision

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Found while reworking #850 (PR #865).

**What happens:** app `pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (heavy lane, `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`). On main, one level's growth plan spends **~200 s in release** in `adaptive/grow.rs`: 33 revolutions, 157 trial steps, about 1.3 s per trial.

**Where the time goes** (local probe, release):
- 99 % of it is `rings::open`, the morphological opening: two `offset_fine` calls at `ARC_TOL` 2.5e-4 mm per trial, plus one per revolution for `whole`.
- The stock walk takes 0.6 s.
- The cleared-area offset and the intersect take 0.2 s each.

The opening's cost grows about with the **square** of the ring's vertex count. Measured cost per (vertices per trial)^2:

| fixture | vertices per trial | ns per (vertices)^2 |
|---|---|---|
| 60 x 14 slot | ~290 | ~63 |
| 60 x 40 island | ~700 | ~105 |
| the bore (fine STEP tessellation) | ~4,700 | ~58 |

So a finely tessellated outline turns a 33-revolution plan into minutes.

**Why it is not bounded:** #850's budget cannot refuse it without changing a plan that finishes on main. Measured on any time-faithful unit, the bore is the most expensive plan of all, so it stays law 2's (length) alone. See `docs/decisions/850-adaptive-geometry-budget.md`.

**Options:**
- Simplify the cleared area and the ring to the planner's working tolerance before the opening. Douglas-Peucker at the `MERGE` / `ARC_TOL` scale would remove the boolean engine's arc-tolerance vertices that say nothing about the shape.
- An opening that does not re-tessellate every convex vertex at `ARC_TOL`.
- An incremental opening.

Each option changes toolpaths: under the safety floor, with every adaptive fixture re-measured.

**Done means:** the bore's growth level plans in seconds (stated bound, release and debug) with the load, crossing and kink laws held. Every adaptive fixture's change is measured and named in the PR.

Related: #850, #44, #845.

body:
Reported by a user in #866 ("Note the 'furniture join'. Seems like AI is hallucinating"), raised by the maintainer, investigated and filed by an agent. Same kind of problem as #876 ("work offset word").

## What "furniture" means
It is this codebase's internal nickname for the things a setup owns that are neither the part's models nor operations: the setup's stock, its WCS (work offset), its fixtures, machine, post and tool list. The source comments use it everywhere (`crates/app/src/setup.rs`, `schema.rs`, `model.rs`: "setup furniture, never a browser row"; `setup::is_furniture_shape`). It is a fair metaphor in comments. It is not a machining term, and no user can know it.

## Where it reached the user (strings, not comments)

title: Theme and colour-vision mode are user preferences, not project state: remember them per user

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
**What happens now**

The theme is document state. `SetTheme` writes a `ThemeRef` singleton into the world, the project file saves it as an optional `theme` key (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs`, written by `project/wire.rs`), and opening a project sets it again (`project/apply.rs`; no key means Dark). So:

- A new document always opens in Dark.
- Each project carries its own theme. Someone who works in Light has to switch every new project, and a colleague's project opens in whatever theme its author used.
- Changing the theme is an undoable edit to the document, and it marks the project as changed.

**Decision (reporter, vilts, 2026-11-11):** the theme and the colour-vision mode are purely user preferences. They have nothing to do with the project, and both survive program restarts.

**Proposed**

- Keep the chosen theme per user, in the OS config folder, the same way recent files already do (#662, `app::recent`: `%APPDATA%`, `~/Library/Application Support`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`; write to a temp file, then rename; a missing or corrupt file starts at the default and says why on the status line, never crashes). Read it at startup and write it when the user picks a theme.
- The project file stops storing the theme. Saving writes no `theme` key. Opening ignores a `theme` key in older files and leaves the user's theme as it is (a compatible read, so no project-file version break is needed for existing documents). Opening a project or File > New never changes the look.
- A missing theme file (a `{"file": path}` preference whose file is gone) keeps the current behaviour: refused by name on the status line, falling back to the built-in default without crashing.
- Theme selection leaves the document's undo history, like the recent-files list (#662: "app PREFERENCE state, not document state"). The pick still goes through one place that validates it (the existing pre-parse in `State::select_theme`), so a corrupt theme is refused at the pick.

**Colour-vision mode too**

The colour-vision mode (`SetColorVision`) is not in the project file and is not saved anywhere, so it resets on every restart. It is kept in the same per-user preference store as the theme, read at startup, and written when the user picks a mode. The startup read still runs the colour-vision gate against the theme it lands on, so a stored mode that fails the gate is refused by name, not applied silently.

**Tests**

The existing theme tests pin the old design and are removed, not updated:
- `project_roundtrip.rs::the_theme_choice_round_trips_and_a_v40_file_means_dark` (the save writes `theme`, and opening applies it)
- `commands_undo.rs::theme_choice_undoes_redoes_and_refuses` (a pick is in the undo history)

Replaced by:
- One project-file test of the new rule: saving writes no `theme` key, and opening an older file that still carries `"theme": {...}` loads cleanly and leaves the user's theme as it was. This guards against a project file overriding the preference again.
- Preference-store tests for theme and colour vision: survives a restart, and a missing or corrupt file starts at the default with a note.

**Done means**

Pick Light, then File > New: the new document is Light. Open a project saved with `"theme": {"named": "dark"}`: it stays Light. Restart the app: still Light. Pick a colour-vision mode, restart: still that mode. Saving a project writes no `theme` key. A corrupt preference file starts in Dark with a status-line note. Tests pin each of these, with the preference store pointed at a temp folder so the suites never touch the real user file.

Labels intended (the filer can't set labels): `enhancement`, `P2`, `effort:medium`, `area:ui`, `source:agent`. Related: #662 (recent files, the store to copy), #698 (light theme), #659.

title: An over-budget STEP mesh is imported at reduced fidelity with only a log line - gouge verdicts on it can pass a real gouge on a convex wall

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
Found in the review of PR #839 (#689).

**What happens.** `crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs` (`shell_facets`, the refinement loop and the `eprintln!` at about lines 188-207) refines a STEP shell toward its chord target. Since #689 that target is `min(extent/1000, 0.005 mm)`. Refinement stops early once the mesh passes `budget / 8` facets (`MAX_FACETS` = 30 M, less what earlier shells used), or when a pass returns `TooLarge`. The importer then keeps the coarser mesh and only prints "step: tessellated at reduced fidelity ..." to stderr. Nothing in the model, the UI, MCP or the program gate records that the mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict assumes.

A related wrinkle: on the `Err(TooLarge) => break` path, `tol` has already been halved while `refined` is the previous, coarser mesh. The log then under-reports the chord error, and if the halved `tol` reaches the target, it says nothing at all.

**Why it matters, in both directions.** The gouge laws judge the program against these facets with a 0.01 mm verdict. A facet is a chord inscribed in the true surface, so it stands inside the material by its sagitta. That cuts both ways:

- **Concave wall** (a bore or a pocket wall): the facets stand toward the tool. A nominal finish reads as a false gouge, which is the safe side. This was the #689 symptom.
- **Convex wall** (a boss or an outside profile): the facets stand away from the tool, so the mesh wall looks farther off than the real wall. A real gouge up to the mesh's actual chord error can pass the verdict. This is the unsafe side.

AGENTS.md, Prime Directive: "if an operation can only be partly computed, mark it 'incomplete' rather than emit a subtly wrong toolpath", and "Log diagnostics, never silence". A stderr line the user never sees is silence.

This risk is not new. Before #689 every STEP mesh was made at `extent/1000`, which is never finer than what an over-budget model gets now. #689 removes the risk for every model that fits the budget. For an over-budget model it remains.

**Options.**
- (a) The import records the chord error it actually achieved on the model, and the gouge laws tighten their floor by the excess over the 0.005 mm cap for that model. That is stricter, never looser; false gouges on concave walls are the safe side.
- (b) The model is flagged "reduced fidelity" visibly in the UI and MCP. The program gate refuses to post operations judged against it until the user acknowledges it or re-imports with a larger budget.
- (c) Both.

**Recommended: (c).** (a) alone keeps the verdict sound but leaves the user wondering about false gouges. (b) alone relies on an acknowledgement.

Done means: an over-budget import is visible to the user and to MCP; no gouge verdict on such a model can be looser than on a full-fidelity one; and tests pin both, including the `TooLarge`-break path's reported chord error.

title: A tool body is judged as two different shapes: the fixture laws sweep its band stack, the reach laws its enclosing cylinder - the simulation can only draw one

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while working #743 part 1 (the simulation draws the tool as the revolved outline the laws judge).

**What happens.** A milling tool with a body (an imported mesh, #368, or a drawn spun holder, #93) is read by the collision laws in two different shapes:

- the fixture laws (`fixture_struck`, `operation::generate` -> `tool_body::stack` -> `verify::steel_stack`) sweep the body's **band stack** - its revolved envelope, up to 32 coaxial bands;
- every law that reads one holder cylinder off `ToolGeom` - law (c), the shank/holder reach against the part and stock walls in `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` (`cx.tool.holder_radius`, `cx.tool.holder_len`), and the probe stack in `verify/probe.rs` - reads the tool `tool_body::judged` returns: the single cylinder **enclosing** the body (`HolderProfile::enclose`): the holder at the body's widest radius from the shank top to the body's top, and the shank widened to the widest the body reaches beside it.

Both are conservative (never smaller than the body), so no collision is missed. But they are not the same shape: for a stepped body (a narrow nose under a wide flange) the enclosing cylinder is the flange's radius all the way down to the shank top.

**Why it matters.** #743 asks that the simulated tool be "the same profile the collision laws judge, so what you see is what is checked". The simulation (PR for #743 part 1) draws the band stack, the tighter of the two and the one the laws that name a fixture collision read. A reach warning from law (c) can therefore fire where the drawn holder is visibly clear of the wall: the user sees a nose 15 mm from the axis, the law judged 40 mm.

**Evidence.** `crates/app/src/tool_body.rs` (`judged`, `stack`), `crates/tools/src/holder_profile.rs` (`enclose`, `stack`), `crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` lines 38-45. `crates/app/tests/tool_spun_profile.rs` already pins the two readings side by side (the enclosing cylinder's radius equals the widest band).

**Options (not decided here).**
1. Law (c) and the other single-cylinder laws read the band stack too (changes verdicts: fewer false reach warnings; under the safety floor, needs its own goldens).
2. Keep the laws; a reach warning from an enclosed body says so in its text ("judged by the cylinder enclosing the body, Ø…"), and the simulation can show that cylinder when such a warning is selected.

Not touched by #743 part 1 - that PR is display only and changes no verdict.

Done means: either every law that judges a tool body reads the same shape the simulation draws (with tests pinning the changed verdicts), or the difference is stated in the warning text and shown on demand, with a test that the drawn shape and the named judged shape agree for each law.

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found by the #817 review (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/817#pullrequestreview-5857229231). The bug is already on main, and it doesn't need a flip.

**Where:** `crates/sim/src/stock_sim/march.rs:241-242`. The arm `phi == 0.0 => Read::Top(z)` treats a probe value of exactly zero as "the probe landed on the surface". But the probe's magnitude belongs to the whole cell, so `phi == 0` only means the cell's **centre** lies on a stock plane. The march then returns whatever height it reached inside that cell.

**Scenario:** a plate from -6.25 to 0 at cell 0.5, so -6.25 sits on a cell centre, with a flat slot at -6.0.

That feeds `march_verdicts` and `columns`. The field engine isn't the default engine, so this is latent today, but it's a silent under-report.

**Fix:** treat `phi == 0` as "this cell's centre is on a surface": refine from the cell, or answer `Unreadable`. Pin it with a fixture whose stock plane sits on a cell centre. The mirrored arms in #817's `march_up.rs` get the same fix there.

Done means: no read under-reports material when a stock plane sits on a cell centre; pinned.

body:
Part of #637 (step E2a; design in https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/issues/637#issuecomment-6787218007, section 3 route (ii)).

The field's lattice is origin-locked (`cell_of(v) = floor(v / cell)`), and a `LatticeTurn`'s signed permutation maps cell `i` to cell `i` or `-i-1` exactly - cell centres onto cell centres. - `bricks`, `cuts`: brick key `(b, slot) -> (-b-1, mirrored slot)` on a negated axis, keys swapped on a quarter turn;
- on a flip, every `cut_ups` record becomes a `cut_downs` record (a new map on the field: "the ray's entry going DOWN from the centre"), and vice versa - the swap IS the record, nothing is recomputed;
- `mesh` facets and `analytic` box transformed exactly; `cost` ledger rebuilt (`region_of`), dirty tracking reset.

title: xtask: the test scanner counts braces inside string literals, so gate test misses tests and quick picks the wrong fn

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
What happens: `cargo xtask gate test <name>` reports `no #[test] fn matches '<name>'` for a test that exists, and the quick tier can attribute a changed test to the wrong function.

Repro on upstream/main (any OS):

```
cargo xtask gate test the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines --dry-run
# no #[test] fn matches 'the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines'
cargo xtask gate test a_bad_library_is_refused_whole_by_name --dry-run
# ok - 1 step
```

Cause: `xtask/src/scan.rs` `test_fns` finds each test's end by counting `{` and `}` characters on every line, including those inside string and char literals. In `crates/app/tests/fixture_library.rs`, `a_bad_library_is_refused_whole_by_name` (line 78) calls `refuse("{", "bad JSON")`. The unbalanced `{` in that string keeps the depth above zero past the test's real closing brace, so its span swallows the next test, `the_library_folder_is_the_override_else_a_sibling_of_machines` (line 111). That test never appears in the scan.

Effects:
- `gate test <name>` cannot run the swallowed test, by name or substring, with or without `--exact`/`--binary`.
- The quick tier picks "the changed #[test] fns of a changed suite" from these spans. A diff inside the swallowed test is attributed to the test before it, so quick can run `--exact` on the wrong fn and report green without running the changed test. (Seen on PR #761: quick reported `app fixture_library (1 fn)` ok while the changed test was the swallowed one.)

Fix direction: skip `{`/`}` inside string literals (`"..."`, with `\"` escapes), raw strings (`r"..."`, `r#"..."#`), char literals (`'{'`) and `//` comments when counting depth. Pin it with an xtask unit test whose fixture has a test containing `"{"` followed by a second test that must be found with the right span.

Done means: both repro commands find their test; the new xtask unit test pins a brace-in-string fixture; the quick tier attributes a change in the second test to the second test.

title: Post gate refuses a Bore at a STEP hole's own size: the sim charges the 0.02 mm facet sagitta as a 20 mm gouge

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
A Bore on a modelled hole, at the hole's own size, is refused by the post gate as a **20 mm gouge**. The operation's own verify finds nothing. The overcut being charged is the gap between the true circle the bore cuts and the inscribed facets of the imported mesh, about 0.02 mm sideways.

**Reproduction** (main b57f8d52, Windows, `camcraft-cli mcp`):

```
import_model   {"path":"testdata/models/Milling-test.step","name":"part"}
set_stock      {"from_model":"part"}
add_tool       {"catalog":"EM-1000-4FL"}
add_operation  {"kind":"bore","tool":"EM-1000-4FL","source":"part","name":"OP"}
detect_holes   {"name":"OP"}        -> 1 hole: xy (0, 0), radius 12.5, entry z 20, floor z 0
generate       {"name":"OP"}        -> status ok, 0 warnings
verify         {}
```

`verify` returns no per-op finding. The program gate says:

```
gouge: program cuts below the model in 1 cell(s), worst 20.00 mm at (4.69, 11.59, z 0.00)
```

(4.69, 11.59) is at r = 12.50, on the hole wall. The same happens with EM-0800-4FL (1 cell, 20.00 mm at (11.76, -4.23)) and EM-0600-4FL (4 cells, 20.00 mm at (9.57, -8.04)).

**Neighbour cases that still work:**
- The same bore with `"stock_to_leave": 0.01` verifies clean, and so do 0.015, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5. With 0.005 it is still refused.
- A 2D Contour around the part's outside (convex walls) on the same finished-part setup passes the gate.

**Root cause (likely):** the STEP mesh is coarser than the gouge verdict.
- `list_features` on the part shows the Ø25 hole wall as 53 flat strips, 6.79° each. The chord sagitta is 12.5 × (1 − cos 3.40°) = **0.022 mm**.
- The STEP importer meshes to a chord tolerance of `extent * 1e-3` (`crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs`, `tol_target`), about 0.06 mm for this 60 mm part.
- The program sim judges against those facets with `tol` = `GOUGE_TOL` = 0.01 mm (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/deviate.rs`, `deviate`). The sideways slack from #299 (`wall_slack.rs`) is the same 0.01 mm.
- On a concave curved wall the facets lie inside the true surface. A bore that cuts the true r = 12.5 therefore removes up to 0.022 mm of "model" between chord and arc. That is past the 0.01 slack, so the column is charged the wall's full 20 mm height.

The sagitta (0.022) against the threshold (stock_to_leave 0.01 plus tol 0.01) matches where the refusal stops. That is why this says "likely" and not "confirmed".

Any finishing pass that meets a concave curved wall at nominal size should hit the same thing: bores, a contour inside a round boss pocket, round internal corners. A larger part has a coarser mesh (extent/1000), so its sagitta is larger.

Done means: a bore at a STEP hole's nominal size verifies clean, a bore 0.05 mm oversize into the same wall is still refused, and both are pinned by tests.

title: Documentation and a browser build of CamCraft on GitHub Pages, built with Zola at each release

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Proposed by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10. **Paused (`P?`) for the maintainer's review**; nothing is picked up until he sets a priority.

## Goal
A public site on GitHub Pages with:
1. **Documentation** (user guide plus developer and architecture docs), generated with **[Zola](https://www.getzola.org/)** (a single binary static site generator, Markdown content, Tera templates, no Node toolchain).
2. **CamCraft in the browser:** the WASM build of the app, published alongside the docs, so a release can be tried without installing anything.

## How it should work
- **Source:** a Zola project in the repo (e.g. `site/`: `config.toml`, `content/`, `templates/`, `static/`). The docs content lives there as Markdown. Existing material is reused where it fits (README sections, `docs/` design notes, release notes).
- **Output folder:** Zola builds into one folder that Pages picks up. Options to decide in review: the `public/` output deployed by the Pages "GitHub Actions" source, or a `gh-pages` branch / `docs/` folder. The site is **regenerated from scratch each release** (no incremental state, no hand-edited output in git).
- **Part of the release cycle:** generating and publishing the site is a step of the minor/major cut (AGENTS.md "A cut goes PR review -> merge to main -> tag"), run on the tagged tree. If it runs on GitHub, it goes in the existing tag-triggered `release.yml`. **No new `push`/`pull_request`/`schedule` trigger** (AGENTS.md Actions budget). It can also be built locally (`zola build`) for previews.
- **Versioned content:** the site shows the version it was built from. Each release overwrites the previous site (one live version); older versions stay in the GitHub releases.
- **WASM app:** the release step builds the app for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (the web build from #31), bundles it (e.g. `wasm-bindgen` + a small loader page, or `trunk`), and places it under the site (e.g. `/app/`), so `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/app/` runs CamCraft in the browser. It is linked from the docs front page with a note on what works in the browser and what doesn't (file access, GPU features).

## Open questions (for the review)
- Pages source: Actions-deployed `public/` vs a branch/folder? (Actions deploy keeps generated files out of git.)
- WASM readiness: #31 says only geometry, CL and post build for wasm32 today. Does this issue wait for #31, or ship docs first and add `/app/` when #31 lands?
- Content scope for the first cut: user guide only, or the developer/architecture section too?
- Relation to #291 (needs-research, which proposed mdBook): this issue picks Zola. On approval, #291's research is folded in here, or #291 is closed as superseded.
- Actions minutes: building the WASM app and the site on the tag run adds billed minutes. Measure and keep it within the budget.

## Done means (once approved and broken down)
- A Zola site in the repo builds locally with `zola build`.
- The release cycle regenerates and publishes it to GitHub Pages at each minor/major cut, with no new CI triggers.
- The published site carries the version and links to the release downloads.
- The WASM build of CamCraft is published under the site and loads in a current browser (once #31 makes the UI build for wasm32).
- AGENTS.md's release steps name the site step.

Related: #291 (documentation site, mdBook proposal), #31 (app and UI on wasm), #72 (release compile targets).

title: Plasma: verification laws for through-cuts - kerf crossing, cut order, rapids, 2D gouge (part of #621)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
**Plasma verification laws: what replaces the gouge and collision checks for a through-cut.**

From [UM10720](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §1.4.2, §4.12.8, §4.13 and the LinuxCNC Plasma Primer §12:
- **Kerf crossing.** A cut path that crosses an already-cut kerf or void (THC dives into the gap, which "can smash the torch into the material") is warned, naming the contour and point. A rapid across a cut-out part's area is warned too (tip-up hazard).
- **Cut order.** A part's inner contours must be cut before the outer that frees it. A violation is refused by name.
- **Rapids.** Rapids run at the operator's G30 Z (no CAM Z). The post must emit G30 after every M205; a missing G30 is a post bug that the law catches.
- **Kerf against the part.** The kerf-offset path must not cut into the part's material, which is the 2D gouge (part geometry versus the kerf band).
- **The 3D stock sim** doesn't run for plasma ops. The verdict is the 2D laws above, stated as such and not silently skipped.

**Done means:** each law is pinned with a fixture that trips it and one that passes; the program verdict blocks the post on a refusal (Prime Directive).

Part of #621

body:
**A PathPilot plasma post for the Tormach 1300PL.**

Words from [UM10720](https://tormach.com/media/asset/u/m/um10720_1300pl_1223a_web.pdf) §6–7 and Tormach's [post guidelines](https://knowledgebase.tormach.com/8l/pathpilot-post-processor-guidelines):
- **Preamble:** `G20|G21 / G90 / G64 P<inch> / G17 / G54.. / G43 H1 / G30`. G64 P is always in inches.
- **Per contour:** `G0` to the lead-in start, then `M200` (AutoFS; or M207/M208/M209/M210/M211 plus F when the op states them), `G15` (probe), `G16` (pierce + THC on), the XY `G1`/`G2`/`G3` path, `M205` (torch off and back to G30 Z), `G30`.
- **End:** `G30` then `M30`.
- **Refused by name:** M3/M4/M5/M7/M8/M9, any Z cutting move, G95/G96.
- **M6 conflict:** the manual's example uses `T1 M6`, but the guidelines list M6 as unsupported on plasma. It's resolved by **omitting M6** and noting it, pending a Hub or real-machine run.
- **No program delimiters** (`%`).

**Done means:**
- the post writes the per-contour block exactly;
- refusals are pinned;
- a golden `.nc` exists for a plate with an outer profile and two holes;
- a PathPilot Hub (1300PL) run is requested from the contributor before trusting it on a machine.
